title: 3D Molecule Generation from Rigid Motifs via $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ Flows
claim: Complex objects can be treated as sets of rigid parts, each placed by a pose and a class label, and generated jointly.
layout: 1 panel, central assembled molecule surrounded by motifs, dotted trajectory lines to labeled points
description: One large rounded gray blob, labeled SE(3) × V_m at the bottom, represents the joint product space of rigid frames and motif classes. An assembled drug-like molecule sits in the centre, drawn as 3D ball-and-stick atoms: black carbon, white hydrogen, blue nitrogen, red oxygen and yellow sulfur. Colored translucent outlines mark each motif: red for benzene, green for isoxazole, blue for amines, pink for methyl and orange for thiocarbonyl. A tan halo around the whole molecule marks it as M_1. Scattered around the blob are the same motifs in unassembled form, each tied to a black dot labeled t_0 by a dotted curve. The dotted curves run to the assembled positions, labeled t_1, M_1^k and M_0^k = (T_0^k, m_0^k). The eye goes first to the central colorful molecule, then follows the dotted trajectories outward.
caption: Molecule $\bm{\mathcal{M}}$ is generated from motifs $\mathcal{M}$ in a joint flow on the product space of rigid frames $T$ and motif classes $m$. Atoms are recovered deterministically from motif frames and canonical poses.
abstract: Three-dimensional molecular structure generation is typically performed at the level of individual atoms, yet molecular graph generation techniques often consider fragments as their structural units. Building on the advances in frame-based protein structure generation, we extend these fragmentation ideas to 3D, treating general molecules as sets of rigid-body motifs. Utilising this representation, we employ SE(3)-equivariant generative modelling for de novo 3D molecule generation from rigid motifs. In our evaluations, we observe results competitive with state-of-the-art bond-implicit methods, surpassing them in atom stability on GEOM-Drugs, while yielding a 2x to 10x reduction in generation steps and 3.5x compression in molecular representations compared to standard atom-based methods. We release our code at https://github.com/rpoletukhin/MotiFlow.
